_comment: Written by `showtime new --from-storyboard`: the plan. Scene ids are the <section> ids in index.html and the ## headings in narration.md. `showtime retime --from-voice` reads it to say where the voice outgrew a shot's planned length.

rows.visual: A line drawing of a fingertip; thousands of faint dots stream straight through it, untouched; a counter "65 billion per second"; on "how do you catch one" the stream keeps going. Frame 0 and the poster: the fingertip with the stream and the type "65 billion per second · Nobel Prize in Physics 2026"
rows.brief: A line drawing of a fingertip; thousands of faint dots stream straight through it, untouched; a counter "65 billion per second"; on "how do you catch one" the stream keeps going. Frame 0 and the poster: the fingertip with the stream and the type "65 billion per second · Nobel Prize in Physics 2026"
rows.narration: About sixty-five billion neutrinos from the Sun pass through your little fingernail every second, and almost none of them touch anything. So how do you catch one?

rows.visual: Name card "Francis Halzen" with the exact citation in quote marks (readable); a line "IceCube Collaboration: about 450 people, 58 institutions, 14 countries"; a drawing of the ice sheet with "South Pole" and the hexagon of strings beneath; then the roadmap bar slides in and stays; step 1 lights
rows.brief: Name card with the exact citation in quote marks (readable); a line ; a drawing of the ice sheet with and the hexagon of strings beneath; then the roadmap bar slides in and stays; step 1 lights
onscreen: IceCube Collaboration: about 450 people, 58 institutions, 14 countries
rows.narration: This year's Nobel Prize in Physics went to Francis Halzen, for decisive contributions to IceCube, a telescope made of Antarctic ice, and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space. Four steps, and three guesses for you.

rows.visual: Step 1 lit. A 1 km block of ice; neutrino arrows cross it untouched. Question card "What are the odds it hits anything in 1 km of ice? (at 100 TeV, our toy model)", timer ring; chips appear after the line: "About 1 in 1,000" / "About 1 in 100,000" / "About 1 in 10 million"
rows.brief: Step 1 lit. A 1 km block of ice; neutrino arrows cross it untouched. Question card , timer ring; chips appear after the line: / /
onscreen: What are the odds it hits anything in 1 km of ice? (at 100 TeV, our toy model)
rows.narration: Step one: the ghost particle. Guess: a high-energy neutrino crosses a whole kilometre of ice. What are the odds it hits anything on the way?

rows.visual: The chance-vs-energy curve from our toy model with 100 TeV marked; "about 1 in {K1}" highlighted; label "our toy model"
rows.brief: The chance-vs-energy curve from our toy model with 100 TeV marked; "about 1 in {K1}" highlighted; label "our toy model"
rows.narration: In our toy model, about one in {K1}. So the detector had to be huge.

rows.visual: Step 2 lit. Schematic: a hot-water drill melts a hole (hose, hot water); a string of sensors drops in; the hexagon fills to 86 strings; on screen "holes melted with hot water", "86 strings · 5,160 sensors", depth marks 1,450 m and 2,450 m
rows.brief: Step 2 lit. Schematic: a hot-water drill melts a hole (hose, hot water); a string of sensors drops in; the hexagon fills to 86 strings; on screen "holes melted with hot water", "86 strings · 5,160 sensors", depth marks 1,450 m and 2,450 m
rows.narration: Step two: the telescope. In nineteen eighty-eight, Halzen and John Learned proposed using the ice itself. Halzen then led the team that built it.

rows.visual: Inside the ice: a neutrino hits a nucleus; a muon flies out leaving a cone of blue light; sensors along the strings light up in time order (colour by time); on screen "Cherenkov light"
rows.brief: Inside the ice: a neutrino hits a nucleus; a muon flies out leaving a cone of blue light; sensors along the strings light up in time order (colour by time); on screen "Cherenkov light"
rows.narration: When one does hit, it makes a charged particle faster than light travels in ice. It leaves a cone of blue light, and each sensor times its arrival.

rows.visual: Step 3 lit; label "our toy model" top-left. The toy example event in 3D on the real IceCube layout: the track, the hits by time, then the fitted direction drawn over the true one. Question card "Space the strings twice as far apart: how much worse does it aim?", ring; chips after the line: "Barely worse (under 1.5x)" / "A few times worse (1.5x to 20x)" / "Over 20 times worse"
rows.brief: Step 3 lit; label top-left. The toy example event in 3D on the real IceCube layout: the track, the hits by time, then the fitted direction drawn over the true one. Question card , ring; chips after the line: / /
onscreen: Space the strings twice as far apart: how much worse does it aim?
rows.narration: Step three: our toy telescope. From the light's arrival times alone, it works out which way the particle was going. Guess: space the strings twice as far apart. How much worse does it aim?

rows.visual: The error-vs-spacing curve from our toy model (Pandel fit), 125 m and 250 m marked, degrees only on the chart; the ratio highlighted; caveat chip top-right "tuned constants: trend only, not IceCube's real aim"
rows.brief: The error-vs-spacing curve from our toy model (Pandel fit), 125 m and 250 m marked, degrees only on the chart; the ratio highlighted; caveat chip top-right "tuned constants: trend only, not IceCube's real aim"
rows.narration: In our toy model, about {T21} times worse: fewer sensors see the light. Trend only, not IceCube's real aim.

rows.visual: Step 4 lit. Card "2013: first evidence of high-energy neutrinos from outer space (4 sigma)"; card "2014: 5.7 sigma"; then the real 6 PeV replay from the public data with "Real event, 8 December 2016", "A shower: the light spreads like a ball, not a cone", "about 6 PeV: almost 1,000 times what the LHC can produce (IceCube)", "time slowed down"
rows.brief: Step 4 lit. Card ; card ; then the real 6 PeV replay from the public data with
onscreen: 2013: first evidence of high-energy neutrinos from outer space (4 sigma)
A shower: the light spreads like a ball, not a cone
about 6 PeV: almost 1,000 times what the LHC can produce (IceCube)
rows.narration: Step four: what it found. In twenty thirteen, IceCube reported the first evidence of high-energy neutrinos from outer space. In twenty sixteen, it caught this shower, replayed from the real data.

rows.visual: A counter "about 100,000 high-energy neutrinos a year"; a jar of identical dots (no colour difference before the reveal); question card "How many come from outer space?", ring; chips after the line: "About half" / "About 1 in 10" / "About 1 in 1,000"
rows.brief: A counter ; a jar of identical dots (no colour difference before the reveal); question card , ring; chips after the line: / /
onscreen: How many come from outer space?
rows.narration: IceCube records about a hundred thousand high-energy neutrinos a year. Guess: how many of them come from outer space?

rows.visual: One dot in a thousand lights up gold: "about 100 (Nobel Committee)"
rows.brief: One dot in a thousand lights up gold: "about 100 (Nobel Committee)"
rows.narration: About a hundred, the Nobel Committee says. The rest are made in our own atmosphere.

rows.visual: An illustrated sky (labelled "illustration"): a diffuse glow; a faint band "our galaxy shines in neutrinos too"; one galaxy circled "NGC 1068: evidence (4.2 sigma), not yet proof"
rows.brief: An illustrated sky (labelled "illustration"): a diffuse glow; a faint band "our galaxy shines in neutrinos too"; one galaxy circled "NGC 1068: evidence (4.2 sigma), not yet proof"
rows.narration: The prize honours that discovery: high-energy neutrinos from space. Which objects make them is still open: one nearby galaxy shows evidence, not yet proof.

rows.visual: Back to the fingertip from shot 1, the stream still passing; cut to the ice: one dot labelled "from space" makes a blue flash among the strings; hold 1.5 s
rows.brief: Back to the fingertip from shot 1, the stream still passing; cut to the ice: one dot labelled "from space" makes a blue flash among the strings; hold 1.5 s
rows.narration: So how do you catch one? With a cubic kilometre of ice, still watching.
